formNote: 좋아하다 is the VERB 'to like (something)', so the thing you like takes the object marker 을/를, not the subject marker 이/가. Add 을 after a consonant (음악을), 를 after a vowel (커피를). The huge English-speaker trap is its adjective cousin 좋다, which means 'is good/likeable' and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 literally says 'coffee is good (to me)', while 커피를 좋아해요 says 'I like coffee' as an action with you as the doer — both translate to English 'I like coffee', but mixing the particles (커피가 좋아해요) is wrong. 좋아하다 conjugates as a regular 하다-style verb: stem 좋아하 + 여요 contracts to 좋아해요 in the 요-form, 좋아합니다 in formal speech. For people, 좋아하다 carries a romantic 'have a crush on' tone (그 사람을 좋아해요 = I have feelings for that person), so to say you merely enjoy someone's company use a softer phrasing. It pairs naturally with hobbies, food, music, and seasons.
usage: 정말/너무 intensify naturally before the verb.
I'm the type who likes exercise.
examples: 저는 김치를 좋아해요.
I like kimchi.
Simple statement of personal preference.
제 동생은 강아지를 정말 좋아해요.
My younger sibling really likes dogs.
Talking about a third person's preference with 정말.
저는 여름보다 겨울을 더 좋아해요.
I like winter more than summer.
Combine with N보다 더 to compare two things.
mistakes: Using 이/가 with 좋아하다: 김치가 좋아해요 is wrong. The verb 좋아하다 needs the object marker, so say 김치를 좋아해요. (Use 이/가 only with the adjective 좋다: 김치가 좋아요.)
Confusing 좋아요 and 좋아해요: 좋아요 = 'it is good / I like it' (adjective, subject = the thing), 좋아해요 = 'I like it' (verb, subject = I). For a person who likes something, prefer 좋아해요.
For people, 좋아해요 can sound romantic. To a friend, 그 친구를 좋아해요 may be heard as 'I have a crush on that friend'; to just mean you get along, rephrase (예: 그 친구랑 잘 맞아요).

english: to go by N / toward N
formNote: The particle (으)로 marks either the MEANS (by what / how) or the DIRECTION (toward which way) of a motion, so 버스로 가요 = 'go by bus' and 오른쪽으로 가요 = 'go to the right'. Attach 로 after a vowel or after the consonant ㄹ (지하철로, 서울로, 사무실로 — 사무실 ends in ㄹ), and 으로 after every other consonant (집으로, 부엌으로). The key contrast for English speakers is 에 vs (으)로: 에 marks a fixed DESTINATION you arrive at (서울에 가요 = go to Seoul, full stop), while (으)로 stresses the ROUTE or HEADING ('toward/in the direction of Seoul', not necessarily stopping there). For transport, English 'by bus' must become 버스로, never 버스에 — 버스에 가요 would weirdly mean 'go onto the bus'. With direction nouns (왼쪽, 이쪽, 위), only (으)로 works. It also collocates with 갈아타다 (지하철로 갈아타요 = transfer to the subway) and means/material more broadly (한국어로 말해요 = speak in Korean).
usage: Means of transport: 로 after a vowel.
Stem ends in ㄹ, so still 로, not 으로.
Direction noun + 으로 after a consonant.
(으)로 also pairs with 오다 for direction.
examples: 저는 버스로 가요.
I go by bus.
Simple: state your means of transport.
시간이 없으니까 택시로 가요.
Let's go by taxi since there's no time.
Everyday: choosing a faster transport.
출구를 나가서 왼쪽으로 쭉 가세요.
Go out the exit and head straight to the left.
Real situation: giving street directions.
mistakes: Using 에 for transport: 버스에 가요 is wrong (it sounds like 'go onto the bus'). For 'by bus' say 버스로 가요; 에 marks the destination, not the vehicle.
Adding the wrong allomorph after ㄹ: 지하철은 ends in ㄹ, so it takes 로, not 으로. Say 지하철로 가요, never 지하철으로 가요.
Confusing 에 (arrival point) with (으)로 (heading): 서울에 가요 = 'go to Seoul', but 서울로 가요 highlights the direction/route 'toward Seoul'. Use 에 when the focus is simply arriving.

english: to go in order to V
formNote: (으)러 attaches to a verb stem to state the PURPOSE of moving, and it is locked to motion verbs only — 가다, 오다, 다니다, 나가다 and the like. Add 러 to a vowel stem (만나러), 으러 to a consonant stem (먹으러); ㄹ stems keep the ㄹ and take 러 (놀러 가요 = go to hang out). The classic English-speaker confusion is (으)러 vs (으)려고: both mean 'in order to', but (으)러 must end in a going/coming verb and names only the errand of that trip (밥 먹으러 가요), whereas (으)려고 works with ANY main verb and expresses broader intention (밥 먹으려고 일찍 왔어요 = 'I came early intending to eat'). Word order matters: the place comes first with 에, then the purpose, then the motion verb — 도서관에 공부하러 가요, not '공부하러 도서관에 가요'-style English ordering. It frequently pairs with everyday errands: 사러(go to buy), 만나러(go to meet), 보러(go to watch a movie), 배우러(go to learn).
usage: I go to meet a friend.
I go to watch a movie.
보다 + 러: a very common outing.
ㄹ stem 놀- keeps ㄹ; pairs with 오다 too.
examples: 점심 먹으러 가요.
I'm going to eat lunch.
Simple: the purpose of a short trip.
도서관에 공부하러 가요.
I go to the library to study.
Everyday: place (에) + purpose + motion verb.
주말에 친구를 만나러 부산에 가요.
This weekend I'm going to Busan to meet a friend.
Real situation: stacking time, purpose, and destination.
mistakes: Using (으)러 with a non-motion verb: 공부하러 해요 is wrong because 하다 isn't a going/coming verb. (으)러 must end in 가다/오다/다니다 etc.; for general intention use (으)려고.
Choosing the wrong allomorph: a consonant stem needs 으러. Say 밥 먹으러 가요, not 밥 먹러 가요.
Forgetting 에 on the place: native order is 도서관에 공부하러 가요. Don't drop the destination particle or put the purpose clause after the motion verb.

formNote: V아/어 보다 means 'do V and see / give V a try', and in the imperative 보세요 it becomes a warm, polite suggestion — exactly what a shopkeeper, host, or friend says when recommending. Build the 아/어 form first: 아 after a stem vowel ㅏ or ㅗ (가 → 가 봐요), 어 otherwise (먹어 봐요), and 해 for 하다 verbs (해 보세요). The biggest pitfall is treating it as a literal command 'try!': it is softer and more inviting than the bare imperative 드세요/가세요, so 먹어 보세요 = 'why don't you give it a taste' rather than a blunt order. Don't confuse the suggestion 보세요 with the past 봤어요, which reports EXPERIENCE ('have you tried/done it before?': 한국 음식 먹어 봤어요?). Note also the homophone trap: 보다 here is the auxiliary 'try', not the main verb 'see/look'. It collocates with food (먹어/마셔 보세요), clothes (입어/신어 보세요), and gentle encouragement (한번 해 보세요 = give it a shot).
usage: 어 form after a non-ㅏ/ㅗ stem.
Standard line in a clothing shop.
하다 → 해; 한번 softens it further.
examples: 이거 한번 먹어 보세요.
Try eating this.
Simple: offering food to a guest.
이 신발 한번 신어 보세요.
Try these shoes on.
Everyday: a clerk inviting you to test shoes.
저 카페에 한번 가 보세요, 분위기가 정말 좋아요.
Try going to that cafe — the atmosphere is really nice.
Real situation: recommending a place with a reason.
mistakes: Picking the wrong vowel: 먹- isn't ㅏ/ㅗ, so it takes 어. Say 먹어 보세요, not 먹아 보세요.
Confusing the suggestion with experience: 먹어 보세요 = 'please try it (now)', but 먹어 봤어요? = 'have you ever tried it (before)?'. Don't use 보세요 to ask about past experience.
Treating it as a blunt order: 보세요 is an invitation, not a command. To politely insist someone eat, 드세요 is more direct; 먹어 보세요 means 'why not give it a try'.

formNote: This is how a Korean ADJECTIVE attaches to a noun in front of it (the modifier always precedes the noun). Add ㄴ to a vowel stem (예쁘다 → 예쁜 가방) and 은 to a consonant stem (작다 → 작은 집); irregulars shift: ㅂ-adjectives like 춥다 become 추운 날씨, ㄹ stems drop ㄹ (길다 → 긴 머리). A core English-speaker trap is that 있다/없다-type 'adjectives' (맛있다, 재미없다) use the VERB-style ending 는, not 은: it's 맛있는 음식, never '맛있은'. Another is mixing this adjective-modifier with the verb-modifier: descriptive states take A-ㄴ/은 (작은 = 'small'), but ongoing actions take V-는 (먹는 = 'eating'). Don't carry over English word order — Korean never says 'a bag pretty'; the adjective sits before the noun with no copula. These modifiers pile up naturally: 작고 예쁜 집 ('a small, pretty house').
usage: 있다-type adjective takes 는, not 은.
examples: 저는 작은 집에 살아요.
I live in a small house.
Simple: one adjective before the noun.
어제 예쁜 가방을 샀어요.
Yesterday I bought a pretty bag.
Everyday: modifier inside a full sentence.
저는 조용하고 깨끗한 카페를 좋아해요.
I like quiet, clean cafes.
Real situation: stacking 조용하- + 깨끗하- before the noun.
mistakes: Using 은 with 있다/없다 adjectives: 맛있은 음식 is wrong. These take the 는 ending — say 맛있는 음식, 재미있는 영화.
Putting the adjective after the noun (English order): 가방 예쁜 is wrong. Korean modifiers come before the noun: 예쁜 가방.
Forgetting irregular changes: 춥다 isn't 춥은. ㅂ-irregular adjectives become 추운, 더운, 매운, etc.

english: a noun that does the verb
formNote: Attach 는 to a verb stem to turn the verb into a present-tense modifier describing the noun behind it: 먹는 사람 = 'a person who is eating / who eats'. This is Korean's equivalent of an English relative clause ('the person WHO eats'), but it sits in FRONT of the noun, so the whole clause is read right-to-left into English. ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ before 는: 살다 → 사는 곳 ('the place where I live'), 알다 → 아는 사람 ('someone I know'). The key tense contrast English speakers must learn: V-는 = present/habitual action (가는 버스 = 'the bus that goes'), V-(으)ㄴ = completed/past (간 사람 = 'the person who went'), V-(으)ㄹ = future/prospective (갈 사람 = 'the person who will go'). Don't confuse this verb 는 with the adjective modifier A-ㄴ/은; only 있다/없다 adjectives borrow the 는 form. Common partners: 사는 곳, 아는 사람, 좋아하는 음식, 자주 가는 가게.
usage: ㄹ stem 살- drops ㄹ → 사는.
examples: 저기 가는 사람이 제 친구예요.
The person going over there is my friend.
Simple: short modifier on a person.
부산에 가는 기차를 탔어요.
I took the train that goes to Busan.
Everyday: the clause includes a destination.
제가 자주 가는 카페는 학교 근처에 있어요.
The cafe I go to often is near the school.
Real situation: a longer relative clause with 자주.
mistakes: Using 는 for a finished action: 'the person who went' is 간 사람, not 가는 사람. Use V-(으)ㄴ for the past, V-는 for present/habitual.
Keeping the ㄹ on ㄹ-stems: 살는 곳 is wrong. The ㄹ drops before 는 — say 사는 곳, 아는 사람.
Translating English word order: don't try 'the bus goes to Busan' as 버스 가는 부산. The clause precedes the noun: 부산에 가는 버스.

english: it seems like N / looks like N
formNote: N 같다 means 'is like N / seems to be N', expressing a resemblance or a soft guess, and the noun sits directly before 같아요 with NO object or subject marker (학생 같아요, never '학생을 같아요'). The adjective 같다 conjugates as a regular ㅏ-stem: 같 + 아요 → 같아요. Two contrasts matter for English speakers. First, 같다 ('same/like') vs 비슷하다 ('similar'): 같다 leans toward 'practically identical / seems to BE it' (쌍둥이 같아요 = 'they're like twins'), while 비슷하다 just means 'roughly alike'. Second, this NOUN-pattern (N 같아요) is a guess about identity or likeness, whereas the VERB/ADJECTIVE pattern V/A-(으)ㄴ/는 것 같아요 expresses a tentative judgment about a situation (비가 오는 것 같아요 = 'it seems to be raining'). A frequent trap is forcing 처럼 here: 처럼 ('like, as') modifies a following verb (천사처럼 웃어요 = 'smiles like an angel'), but to predicate 'it seems like an angel' you need 천사 같아요. Collocates with impressions: 꿈 같아요, 거짓말 같아요, 진짜 같아요.
usage: A soft guess about someone's identity.
examples: 저 사람은 학생 같아요.
That person seems like a student.
Simple: guessing someone's identity.
오늘 날씨는 봄 같아요.
Today's weather feels like spring.
Everyday: comparing a season to the current feel.
이 그림이 너무 진짜 같아서 사진인 줄 알았어요.
This painting looks so real I thought it was a photo.
Real situation: resemblance leading to a mistaken impression.
mistakes: Adding 을/를 before 같아요: 학생을 같아요 is wrong. 같다 takes no object marker — say 학생 같아요.
Using 처럼 instead: 천사처럼 같아요 is wrong/redundant. Use 천사 같아요 to predicate 'seems like an angel'; 처럼 goes with a following verb (천사처럼 웃어요).
Mixing up identity vs situation guesses: for 'it seems to be raining' say 비가 오는 것 같아요, not 비 같아요. Use N 같아요 only for likeness to a noun.

formNote: 보다 is the comparison particle 'than', and it attaches to the STANDARD you measure against (the thing being beaten), then 더 ('more') plus the adjective: 저보다 더 커요 = 'taller than me'. A frequent English-speaker error is attaching 보다 to the wrong side — in '오늘은 어제보다 더 추워요', the topic 오늘 is what's colder and 어제 (yesterday) is the baseline with 보다, mirroring English 'today is colder THAN yesterday'. 더 is often optional and idiomatic (어제보다 추워요 already implies 'colder'), but adding 더 sounds natural and emphatic; its opposite 덜 means 'less' (어제보다 덜 추워요 = 'less cold than yesterday'). For the superlative 'the most', switch to 제일/가장 (제일 커요 = 'the biggest'). Don't use 보다 with a 'than' clause the English way before a verb — Korean keeps it as 'N보다'. It collocates with size, speed, weather, and quantity: 키가 커요, 빨라요, 더워요, 많아요.
usage: 보다 attaches to the baseline 저 (me).
Swap 더 for 덜 to mean 'less'.
examples: 저는 동생보다 키가 커요.
I'm taller than my sibling.
Simple: 보다 marks the person you outdo.
오늘은 어제보다 더 추워요.
Today is colder than yesterday.
Everyday: 더 emphasizes the bigger degree.
지하철이 버스보다 훨씬 더 빨라서 지하철로 가요.
The subway is much faster than the bus, so I'll go by subway.
Real situation: 훨씬 ('much') intensifies the comparison.
mistakes: Attaching 보다 to the subject instead of the standard: for 'I'm taller than my sibling' say 저는 동생보다 커요, not 동생은 저보다 커요 (that reverses the meaning). 보다 marks what you're compared against.
Using 보다 for the superlative: 'the tallest' is 제일/가장 커요, not 보다 커요. 보다 compares two things; 제일/가장 picks the top of a group.
Forgetting irregular adjective forms: 빠르다 becomes 빨라요 (르-irregular) and 덥다 becomes 더워요 (ㅂ-irregular). Say 버스보다 빨라요, not 버스보다 빠르요.

formNote: V기로 하다 reports a DECISION or resolution to do something; 기 nominalizes the verb, 로 marks it as the chosen course, and 하다 ('to do/decide') is kept in the past 했어요 because the deciding already happened — even when the action itself is future (내일 가기로 했어요 = 'I('ve) decided to go tomorrow'). Attach 기로 했어요 straight to the plain stem (가기로, 배우기로, 운동하기로); for the negative, put 안 before the verb (안 먹기로 했어요 = 'decided not to eat'). The main English-speaker pitfall is conjugating 하다 to the future (가기로 할 거예요 is a different nuance: 'I'm going to decide') or to the present (가기로 해요 sounds like a soft proposal 'let's decide to go'); for an already-settled plan, lock it in the past: 했어요. Contrast with V(으)ㄹ게요, which is an on-the-spot promise/volition ('I'll do it', 제가 갈게요), whereas 기로 했어요 reports a decision reached beforehand, often a mutual or deliberate one. It collocates with resolutions and arrangements: 같이 가기로 했어요, 끊기로 했어요, 매일 운동하기로 했어요.
usage: 하다 verb; a New Year's-style resolution.
Negative: 안 goes before the verb.
examples: 저는 한국어를 배우기로 했어요.
I've decided to learn Korean.
Simple: announcing a personal decision.
내년에 한국에 가기로 했어요.
I've decided to go to Korea next year.
Everyday: a future plan kept in past 했어요.
건강을 위해서 오늘부터 커피를 끊기로 했어요.
For my health, I've decided to quit coffee starting today.
Real situation: a resolution with a reason and a start point.
mistakes: Conjugating 하다 to match a future action: 내일 가기로 할 거예요 changes the meaning to 'I'm going to decide'. For a settled plan keep the past: 내일 가기로 했어요.
Putting 안 in the wrong spot for the negative: say 안 먹기로 했어요 ('decided not to eat'), not 먹기로 안 했어요 (which sounds like 'didn't decide to eat').
Confusing it with (으)ㄹ게요: 제가 갈게요 is an on-the-spot promise, while 가기로 했어요 reports a decision already made. Use 했어요 for a plan you settled earlier.

formNote: 동안 is a duration noun meaning 'the span / while', placed after a time-length noun to say how long something lasts: 한 시간 동안 = 'for one hour', 방학 동안 = 'during the vacation'. No particle goes between the noun and 동안 (한 시간 동안, never '한 시간에 동안'). The crucial English-speaker contrast is 동안 vs 에: 에 pins an action to a POINT in time ('AT 3 o'clock', 세 시에 갔어요), while 동안 stretches it over a STRETCH of time ('FOR three hours'). So 'I studied for three hours' is 세 시간 동안 공부했어요, but 'I studied at three' is 세 시에 공부했어요. With a verb clause it becomes V-는 동안 ('while ~ing': 제가 자는 동안 = 'while I sleep'). Also distinguish 동안 (a duration) from 까지 (a deadline 'until'): 'until 3' is 세 시까지, 'for 3 hours' is 세 시간 동안 — English 'for' here is NOT 위해(서). It collocates with study, travel, waiting, and stays: 공부했어요, 여행했어요, 기다렸어요, 살았어요.
usage: A period of time as the span.
examples: 한 시간 동안 기다렸어요.
I waited for one hour.
Simple: stating how long an action lasted.
방학 동안 한국에 갔다 왔어요.
I went to Korea (and came back) during the vacation.
Everyday: an event filling a period.
제가 자는 동안 친구가 전화를 했더라고요.
While I was sleeping, my friend (apparently) called.
Real situation: V-는 동안 with a clause.
mistakes: Adding a particle before 동안: 한 시간에 동안 is wrong. Nothing goes between the noun and 동안 — say 한 시간 동안.
Using 에 (a point) for a span: 'I studied for three hours' is 세 시간 동안 공부했어요, not 세 시에 공부했어요 (that means 'studied AT three'). Use 동안 for duration.
Confusing 동안 ('for/during') with 까지 ('until'): 'open for 3 hours' is 세 시간 동안, but 'open until 3' is 세 시까지. Don't translate every English 'for' the same way.
